# Asymmetric single outer pair: exact symmetric-middle theorem and an ordinary tail bridge

This note removes the reflection requirement from the four-fiber theorem when the common middle body is centrally symmetric. It then states the exact scalar inequality sufficient for the smaller OC payment with an arbitrary middle body. That scalar inequality is an OPEN bridge here, not a proved theorem. The separate six-interval example shows why a single-pair proof cannot simply be summed.

## 1. Exact four-fiber theorem without any endpoint relation

Let d>=1, let B=-B be a full-dimensional convex body of volume b, and let A,D be arbitrary convex bodies contained in B with the SAME d-volume a. They need not be translates, reflections, or homothetic. At bases -1,0,1,2 take the fibers

    A, B, B, D.                                    (1)

Their canonical convex hull has exactly those four fibers: it is contained in R times B, includes the two full B slices, and the endpoint base planes expose precisely A,D. Its projection is [-1,2], so it is lattice complete. Define raw depth D_S(Y)=inf_{H containing Y} mu(H), and put M=2(b+a).

Then the EXACT mixed maximum is

    max_{Y in S} D_S(Y)=b/2+a.                     (2)

Both middle marks (0,0),(1,0) attain it.

### Lower bound for every actual halfspace

Take a nonvertical through-(0,0) cap u·x>=tz, u!=0. The own B fiber contributes b/2. If t>=0, the missed part of A at base -1 is

    A intersect{u·x<-t} subset B intersect{u·x<-t}.

By central symmetry the volume of the latter set is exactly the volume of the OTHER middle cap B intersect{u·x>=t}. Thus that middle cap pays the entire missed part of A, giving combined contribution at least a. The D contribution is nonnegative and may be retained without expenditure.

If t<0, use D at base2 instead. Its missed part is contained in B intersect{u·x<2t}, of volume at most b/2. The other-middle cap B intersect{u·x>=t} has volume at least b/2, so it again pays the entire missed part. Therefore all these caps have mass at least b/2+a. Pure-base caps contain the own B and at least one entire exterior body, so have mass at least b+a. Every containing cap contains a parallel through-point cap.

The proof at (1,0) follows by reversing the base order and interchanging A,D. No continuous reflection of the outer bodies is used.

### Matching global upper cover

Fix any nonzero u and choose L>0 sufficiently large. The pair

    ±u·x-Lz>=0                                    (3)

contains the whole A, cuts the own B at0 exactly in half, and misses the other two fibers. Each cap has mass a+b/2; their margins sum to -2Lz, so their union covers every continuous point over every z<=0.

Likewise the pair

    ±u·x+L(z-1)>=0                                (4)

has the same mass, capturing D and half of B at1, and their union covers every plane over z>=1. The four caps cover ALL integer planes globally. This proves (2), retaining every competing source and every continuous mark.

## 2. Finite equal-ratio contraction with independent endpoint anchors

Choose arbitrary c_A in A and c_D in D and set

    A_t=c_A+(1-t)(A-c_A),
    D_t=c_D+(1-t)(D-c_D),     0<=t<=1.

Each remains in B; their common volume is a_t=(1-t)^d a. Thus compatibility, completeness, and the exact all-cap formula persist:

    beta(t)=(b/2+a_t)/[2(b+a_t)].                  (5)

This decreases strictly with t when a>0 and t<1, because d beta/da_t=b/[4(b+a_t)^2]>0. At t=1 the endpoint fibers are independently chosen points of zero d-volume and zero depth; the two positive adjacent B fibers have normalized maximum1/4. This generalizes the reflected-endpoint path: no synchronization of the endpoint centers is required, only their volume scale.

## 3. Exact ordinary scalar bridge for an arbitrary middle body

Now let B be arbitrary, with centroid0 and volume b, and retain A,D subset B of equal volume a. These data still give an actual four-fiber body (1). For a continuous direction u define

    P(s)=|B intersect{u·x>=s}|.

Consider the candidate (0,0). When t<0, its two middle traces alone have mass P(0)+P(t)>=2 Gamma_d b>=Gamma_d(b+a), by ordinary Grünbaum and a<=b. When t>=0, its left A trace is at least

    [a-|B intersect{u·x<-t}|]_+
        =[a-b+P(-t)]_+.

Ignoring only the nonnegative D contribution therefore gives the exact bound

    cap mass >=P(0)+P(t)+[a-b+P(-t)]_+.           (6)

For fixed B,u,t, the right side of (6) minus Gamma_d(b+a) is a convex piecewise-affine function of a in [0,b], minimized at a=b-P(-t). Consequently the precise sufficient parallel-tail inequality is

    P(0)+P(t)+Gamma_d P(-t)>=2 Gamma_d b,
                t>=0.                            (7)

If (7) holds for every direction of B, the two actual middle centroids each pay Gamma_d(b+a), hence normalized Gamma_d/2. No conclusion about (7) is assumed in this note.

The reduction is sharp for this candidate and this one-pair construction. If (7) fails at B,u,t, take

    A=D=B intersect{u·x<=-t}.

Both endpoint bodies have volume a=b-P(-t). For t>0 their traces in the cap u·x>=tz at bases -1 and2 have zero volume, so its exact mass is P(0)+P(t), below Gamma_d(b+a). Thus a violation of the ordinary scalar bridge yields an ACTUAL compatible four-fiber counterexample to the middle-centroid candidate. It would not by itself exclude some different optimal mixed mark.

For centrally symmetric B, Section1 already proves the stronger exact conclusion (2). Section3 is a distinct bridge for asymmetric B, not a rephrasing of arbitrary mixed-dimensional OC.

## 4. Transport domination requires a monotone coupling

For a farther equal-volume pair A_k,D_k at bases -k,k+1, a transport T:A_k->D_k gives two interpolants

    m_0(X)=((k+1)X+k T(X))/(2k+1),
    m_1(X)=(k X+(k+1)T(X))/(2k+1).

Actual compatibility puts these in B. If T is a differentiable injective volume-preserving monotone map with positive semidefinite derivative, then det DT=1 and

    det((1-theta)I+theta DT)>=1,    0<=theta<=1,

by the weighted arithmetic-geometric mean inequality on its nonnegative eigenvalues. The pushforwards of Lebesgue measure under m_0,m_1 therefore have densities at most1_B. This statement is conditional on that specified map; no regularity theorem for a general transport is needed here.

For arbitrary volume-preserving couplings the domination is false. For example T(X)=-X on a centrally symmetric A_k=D_k contracts m_0,m_1 by the factor1/(2k+1), producing densities (2k+1)^d on their images. Thus mass preservation of endpoints alone must not be confused with density control of interpolated measures.

Even the monotone, unit-density version does not settle collective allocation. In the six-interval body of `candidate bf54b5b745d6332c`, the monotone equal-interval maps are identities. Both interpolants are precisely the original outer intervals with density1, but the near/far pairs overlap at the lower end. That example disproves the full-pair credit despite this individual domination; the smaller Gamma_d(b+sum a_k) payment remains open here.
